system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2147-09-24 22:38:00 to 2147-09-26 18:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, gastroparesis, chronic abdominal pain, depression, anxiety, and recurrent UTIs was admitted for nausea, vomiting, abdominal and back pain, and dysuria. She had elevated blood pressure, acute kidney injury with creatinine of 2.6, hyperglycemia, and leukocytosis. Imaging showed no renal abnormalities. Symptoms were attributed to dehydration causing acute kidney injury and a flare of chronic gastroparesis. IV fluids led to improvement in kidney function and symptoms. Her home medications, including insulin, anti-nausea, pain, and psychiatric medications, were continued. Lisinopril was held initially but restarted as renal function improved. Antibiotics were not continued due to lack of clear infection and prior resistance. She stabilized, resumed oral intake, and was discharged home with instructions to follow up for kidney function and medication management.
problems: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic autonomic (poly)neuropathy
Elevated white blood cell count, unspecified
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ women with history of IDDM, GERD, HTN, 
depression, chronic leukocytosis, chronic back pain, recurrent 
UTIs, and multiple hospitalizations for abdominal pain with PO 
intolerance of unclear etiology (but possibly secondary to 
gastroparesis and anxiety) who presents with nausea and vomiting 
and abdominal pain concerning for gastroparesis flare.

ACTIVE ISSUES:

# Acute on chronic abdominal pain
Patient has known delayed gastric emptying in the setting of 
poorly controlled DM. There is also suspicion for a component of 
functional abdominal pain secondary to anxiety as treatment with 
benzodiazepines during prior hospitalizations, in the absence of 
any other acute pathology, have appeared to alleviate her 
pain/anxiety. There was low suspicion of infection as patient 
was afebrile, had downtrending WBC, and had no localizing 
symptoms or signs of infection. Patient was treated with 
Tylenol, tramadol, lorazepam, and ondansetron, haloperidol, and 
IV fluids. At the time of discharge, patient was able to 
tolerate PO fluids and full meals.

# Leukocytosis
Patient has chronically elevated WBC at baseline. On admission 
her WBC was 23.1, downtrending to 19.5 and then 13.3 after 
admission to the medicine floor.

# Asymptomatic bacteriuria
Patient has history of recurrent UTIs and is known to be 
colonized with MDR organisms including Klebsiella. Her UA on 
admission was consistent with bacteriuria, but in the absence of 
urinary symptoms and fevers, she was not treated with 
antibiotics.

# Acute kidney injury, resolving
Patient was not able to tolerate PO intake for two days prior to 
admission. Initial Cr was 1.6, down to baseline 1.3 on the day 
of discharge with IV fluids and improved PO intake.

# Hypertensive urgency, resolved
BP up to systolic 250 in emergency department, likely in the 
setting of agitation in the ED. This resolved following 
administration of Ativan and Haldol. Home antihypertensives were 
initially held for normotension, then resumed at discharge 
except for lisinopril given recent kidney injury.

CHRONIC ISSUES:
# Diabetes mellitus type 2
Patient has poorly controlled insulin-dependent diabetes. In the 
hospital, she had finger stick blood glucose up to 300s but 
without evidence of DKA. Most likely due to poor adherence to 
home medication regimen. Continued Lantus and Humalog sliding 
scale.

nifedipine, propranolol, and isosorbide. Home Lisinopril was 
held due to soft BPs on ___ and mild ___ on admission.

# Anxiety

lorazepam at home. These medications were continued on home 
doses.

poorly controlled DM. There is also suspicion for a component of 
functional abdominal pain secondary to anxiety as treatment with 
benzodiazepines during prior hospitalizations, in the absence of 
any other acute pathology, have appeared to alleviate her 
pain/anxiety. There was low suspicion of infection as patient 
was afebrile, had downtrending WBC, and had no localizing 
symptoms or signs of infection. Patient was treated with 
Tylenol, tramadol, lorazepam, and ondansetron, haloperidol, and 
IV fluids. At the time of discharge, patient was able to 
tolerate PO fluids and full meals.

# Leukocytosis
Patient has chronically elevated WBC at baseline. On admission 
her WBC was 23.1, downtrending to 19.5 and then 13.3 after 
admission to the medicine floor.

# Asymptomatic bacteriuria
Patient has history of recurrent UTIs and is known to be 
colonized with MDR organisms including Klebsiella. Her UA on 
admission was consistent with bacteriuria, but in the absence of 
urinary symptoms and fevers, she was not treated with 
antibiotics.

# Acute kidney injury, resolving
Patient was not able to tolerate PO intake for two days prior to 
admission. Initial Cr was 1.6, down to baseline 1.3 on the day 
of discharge with IV fluids and improved PO intake.

# Hypertensive urgency, resolved
BP up to systolic 250 in emergency department, likely in the 
setting of agitation in the ED. This resolved following 
administration of Ativan and Haldol. Home antihypertensives were 
initially held for normotension, then resumed at discharge 
except for lisinopril given recent kidney injury.

CHRONIC ISSUES:
# Diabetes mellitus type 2
Patient has poorly controlled insulin-dependent diabetes. In the 
hospital, she had finger stick blood glucose up to 300s but 
without evidence of DKA. Most likely due to poor adherence to 
home medication regimen. Continued Lantus and Humalog sliding 
scale.

# Hypertension
At the time of discharge, patient was on home doses of 
nifedipine, propranolol, and isosorbide. Home Lisinopril was 
held due to soft BPs on ___ and mild ___ on admission.

# Depression
# Anxiety
Patient takes sertraline, amitriptyline, pregabalin, and 
lorazepam at home. These medications were continued on home 
doses.

# GERD
Patient was continued on home omeprazole and sucralfate

TRANSITION ISSUES:
- Please check basic metabolic panel at outpatient followup, to 
ensure stability of creatinine.
- Lisinopril was held at discharge due to mostly normotensive 
BPs during hospitalization and ___ (which was improving on day 
of discharge). Please resume as outpatient if appropriate.
- Patient has multiple hypo- and hyper-pigmented lesions on both 
breasts which started as tender, pus-filled pockets three weeks 
ago. Consider referral to dermatologist for further workup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been throwing up non-stop for three days. I can’t keep anything down. My stomach hurts, and I feel really weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just chills, no fever. I’ve been so nauseous I haven’t taken my meds or eaten in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We know from your labs that your blood sugar was high when you arrived—369—and your kidney function was a bit off, with creatinine at 1.6. But it looks like you’re not in diabetic ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from not taking my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. When you’re vomiting, it’s hard to keep meds down, and that can spike your sugars. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to help stabilize things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. It feels like my gastroparesis acting up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s what we suspect. Your history shows multiple episodes like this—nausea, vomiting, inability to eat—likely due to delayed stomach emptying from your diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s scary every time. I get so anxious when the pain starts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that in the ER. Your blood pressure was very high—up to 250—and you were agitated. The team gave you Ativan and Haldol, which helped calm you and bring your BP down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. I felt out of control. But I’m feeling more relaxed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also treating your pain with Tylenol and tramadol, and ondansetron for nausea. You’ve got a central line in your right groin because your veins are hard to access—we’ll remove it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your labs. Your white blood cell count is high—23.1—but it’s been high in the past, and it’s already starting to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. You don’t have a fever or urinary symptoms. Your urine test showed some bacteria, but the culture came back as contamination—probably from skin or genital flora. So we’re not treating it with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many UTIs. I thought this might be another one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’re prone to them, but this doesn’t look like an active infection. Treating without clear signs could lead to resistance, so we’re holding off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. My stomach still hurts a little, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs this morning show improvement. Creatinine is down to 1.3—back to your baseline. Your blood sugar is 126, and your white count dropped to 13.3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my kidneys are okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The kidney injury was likely due to dehydration from not eating or drinking. IV fluids helped reverse that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood pressure meds? I take lisinopril, nifedipine, propranolol…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held the lisinopril because of the kidney issue, but you’re on your other BP meds—nifedipine and propranolol. Your pressures have been stable, in the 110s to 130s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart lisinopril when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding it for now. Your PCP should check your kidney function first and decide if it’s safe to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on your full insulin regimen—Lantus at night and Humalog with meals. We’ll make sure you have prescriptions before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like you to try some food—maybe a light meal. If you can keep it down, that’s a big step toward going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard you ate most of your lunch and didn’t vomit. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did! Just a little at a time, but it stayed down. I feel like I can breathe easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ve tolerated full meals, your labs are improving, and you’re in much less pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. But what about the spots on my breasts? They started as painful bumps three weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. They’re a mix of light and dark patches, possibly from an old infection. We’re recommending a dermatology referral—your PCP can set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up. And I should see my PCP about my stomach and meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll check your kidney function, review your medications, and help manage your gastroparesis and anxiety. Keep using lorazepam as needed for anxiety—it’s part of your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad I can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove your central line now. You’ll need to keep the site clean and dry for 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No showering right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. You’re going home on all your usual meds except lisinopril, which is on hold. Please follow up with your PCP within the week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we hope you stay feeling better.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, gastroparesis, anxiety, and recurrent abdominal pain was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain lasting three days. She had been unable to eat or take medications, leading to hyperglycemia and acute kidney injury with creatinine rising to 1.6. In the ED, she was agitated with hypertensive urgency, managed with Ativan and Haldol. IV fluids, insulin, antiemetics, and pain control were initiated. Her symptoms improved, she tolerated oral intake, and labs showed resolution of kidney injury and downtrending white count. Asymptomatic bacteriuria was noted but not treated. Lisinopril was held due to recent kidney injury. She was discharged home with instructions to follow up with her PCP for medication management and a dermatology referral for breast lesions.
